--- ABSTRACT ---
[BACKGROUND]: The transient rise in blood lipids following a high-fat meal (HFM), known as postprandial lipemia, is linked to systemic inflammation and cardiovascular disease, but can be blunted by exercise. However, minimal research has investigated the effects of realistic exercise bouts on postprandial lipemia and inflammation in at-risk individuals. The purpose of this study was to assess the effects of moderate-intensity aerobic exercise lasting 30 or 60 min performed the evening before a HFM, on postprandial lipemia and inflammation in overweight, insufficiently active men.
[METHODS]: In this randomized-crossover study, twelve participants remained sedentary (CON), or performed a brisk walk on a treadmill at 60 % VO2peak for either 30 min (EX-30) or 60 min (EX-60), after which they consumed a small snack (270 kcal) to partially replace exercise energy expenditure. Following a 12-h overnight fast, participants consumed a standard HFM (1 g fat/kg; 1 g CHO/kg; 1117.8 ± 117.0 kcal). Blood draws were performed at baseline (pre-HFM) and 1, 2, 4, 6, and 8 h post-HFM to assess glucose, insulin, lipids, and systemic inflammation.
[RESULTS]: There were no significant differences (p > 0.05) in fasting triglycerides between EX-60 (118.7 ± 68.3 mg/dL), CON (134.8 ± 66.2 mg/dL) or EX-30 (135.5 ± 85.4 mg/dL). There were no differences in peak, time-to-peak, total or incremental area-under-the-curve between trials for triglyceride response (p > 0.05). There was no significant main effect of time (p > 0.05) in IL-1ra, IL-4, IL-5, IL-6, IL-10 or TNF-α from baseline to 8 h post-HFM in any trial.
[CONCLUSIONS]: In summary, we found that in overweight, insufficiently active men, neither 30 nor 60 min of moderate-intensity exercise performed 12 h prior to a HFM attenuated postprandial lipemia or inflammation, which could potentially be explained by the partial caloric replacement of exercise energy expenditure.

key_findings.finding: In a randomized 3-condition crossover of 9 healthy men, 60 min treadmill walking at 50% VO2peak (~520 kcal) followed by glucose replacement (~130 g, replacing the estimated exercise expenditure) did not increase subsequent postprandial lipemia: total and incremental triglyceride AUC were significantly lower versus resting control, with no difference between glucose-replaced exercise and unreplaced exercise. This directly argues against glucose energy replacement increasing lipemia after moderate exercise (PMID 25424502).

key_findings.finding: In 8 recreationally active men, a more demanding exercise bout (90 min cycling at 70% VO2peak plus ten 1-min maximal sprints) lowered postprandial TG by 40% without carbohydrate replacement, whereas glucose solutions given at 0, 2, and 4 h postexercise to restore carbohydrate/energy balance abolished the exercise-related lipid benefit; effects were not evident in the replacement condition versus control. Thus replacement attenuated rather than increased lipemia relative to control, while unreplaced exercise produced the lowest TG (PMID 19112157).

source_tools.relevance: Abstract directly reports exercise protocol, glucose timing, replacement condition, and TG direction.

key_findings.finding: In 13 overweight/obese men, walking at 50% maximal oxygen uptake with a net expenditure of 27 kJ/kg reduced postprandial TG by 14% versus control and 10% versus energy-replacement; replacement still altered insulin and fat oxidation but the energy deficit was necessary to lower postprandial lipemia. This supports no increase from replacement, but a loss/attenuation of the exercise-induced TG reduction (PMID 17998903).

source_tools.relevance: Abstract specifies moderate intensity, crossover control/deficit/replacement design, and TG comparisons.

key_findings.finding: In 18 healthy boys, exercise at 60% peak VO2 followed either by immediate replacement of the 32 kJ/kg exercise expenditure or no replacement, the unreplaced condition reduced total postprandial TAG AUC by 15% versus control and 16% versus replacement; replacement and control were similar. Immediate energy replacement therefore negated the benefit but did not increase lipemia above control (PMID 26975542).

key_findings.finding: A moderate-intensity study in 12 overweight/inactive men (60% VO2peak, 30 or 60 min) provided a 270-kcal snack after exercise, only partially replacing expenditure; neither exercise condition differed from sedentary control in TG peak or total/incremental AUC. This is compatible with attenuation or null effect, not an increase, but the snack was not glucose-specific and replacement was partial (PMID 27366132).
